summary.title: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay
summary.authors: Zejun Wang, Jiawen Zhou, Yiheng Zhang, Weiya Zhu, Yuan Li
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science; Organic Chemistry; Photothermal Conversion
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the challenge of synthesizing stable, open-shell organic radicals for photothermal applications, which are typically unstable in air due to unsatisfied valency. The authors introduce a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs), specifically TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8, synthesized via facile demethylation and oxidation of phenolic precursors. These materials exhibit high electrochemical and thermal stability due to rich resonance structures, including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide forms. A key finding is that these ANARs possess extremely high spin concentrations and highly enhanced nonradiative decay, which suppresses fluorescence and boosts photothermal conversion. Among the tested molecules, TPA-TPA-O6 demonstrates superior performance, with a temperature rise from 25 °C to 210 °C within 60 seconds under 808 nm laser irradiation. When integrated into a polyurethane (PU) foam interface for solar-driven water evaporation, TPA-TPA-O6 achieves a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and an evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun illumination. This performance is competitive with top-tier organic photothermal materials and superior to many inorganic counterparts in terms of solubility and reproducibility. The study further validates the practical utility of TPA-TPA-O6 for seawater desalination, showing significant reduction in primary ion concentrations. The work establishes a novel strategy for designing stable, small-molecule organic photothermal materials with restricted radiative decay, offering a cost-effective and scalable alternative to complex conjugated polymers or inorganic nanomaterials.

High spin concentration correlates with enhanced photothermal performance.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the challenge of synthesizing stable, open-shell organic radicals for photothermal applications, which are typically unstable in air due to unsatisfied valency. The authors introduce a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs), specifically TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8, synthesized via facile demethylation and oxidation of phenolic precursors. These materials exhibit high electrochemical and thermal stability due to rich resonance structures, including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide forms. A key finding is that these ANARs possess extremely high spin concentrations and highly enhanced nonradiative decay, which suppresses fluorescence and boosts photothermal conversion. Among the tested molecules, TPA-TPA-O6 demonstrates superior performance, with a temperature rise from 25 °C to 210 °C within 60 seconds under 808 nm laser irradiation. When integrated into a polyurethane (PU) foam interface for solar-driven water evaporation, TPA-TPA-O6 achieves a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and an evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun illumination. This performance is competitive with top-tier organic photothermal materials and superior to many inorganic counterparts in terms of solubility and reproducibility. The study further validates the practical utility of TPA-TPA-O6 for seawater desalination, showing significant reduction in primary ion concentrations. The work establishes a novel strategy for designing stable, small-molecule organic photothermal materials with restricted radiative decay, offering a cost-effective and scalable alternative to complex conjugated polymers or inorganic nanomaterials.

Research Context
Open-shell organic radicals have attracted attention for applications in optoelectronics and photothermal conversion. Most open-shell radicals are thermodynamically or kinetically unstable in air. Inorganic photothermal materials often contain precious metals and pose safety issues. Conjugated polymers and 2D frameworks suffer from poor synthesis reproducibility. Organic small molecules are overlooked due to cumbersome synthesis and poor stability. Stable neutral radicals are challenging to prepare due to reactivity with oxygen. Previous work on stable radicals inspired the design of aromatic nitric acid radicals.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to synthesize stable aromatic nitric acid radicals without steric hindrance groups. It is hypothesized that these radicals will exhibit high electrochemical and thermal stability. The authors predict that high spin concentration will enhance nonradiative decay. The central question is whether these radicals can achieve efficient photothermal conversion. It is expected that TPA-TPA-O6 will show superior performance due to its structure. The hypothesis includes that these materials will be suitable for solar-driven water evaporation. The study seeks to verify if restricted radiative decay leads to high efficiency.

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials were synthesized: TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8. Synthesis involved facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. Characterization included cyclic voltammetry (CV), UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, and electron spin resonance (ESR). CV tests were conducted in dichloromethane with 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 as supporting electrolyte. The scan rate for CV measurements was 0.1 V/s. Precursors were dissolved at a concentration of 5 mg/mL. ESR spectra were measured at a test amount of 0.02 mmol. Photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) was tested in dichloromethane solution and film. An interface heating evaporation system was established using white polyurethane (PU) foam. TPA-TPA-O6 was loaded into PU foam by impregnation and drying at 80 °C. The foam diameter was 2.0 cm with 30 mg of TPA-TPA-O6 loading. Solar irradiation was 1 sun (1 kW m⁻²) for evaporation tests.

Procedures And Architectures
The materials are star-shaped with cores like triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene. The radicals feature closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide resonance structures. UV-Vis absorption of TPA-TPA-O6 film shows a red shift with a tail to 825 nm. The powder of TPA-TPA-O6 is totally black, indicating wide visible absorption. HOMO energy levels were calculated from CV curves. HOMO levels for TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8 are -4.90, -4.81, -4.97, and -4.84 eV. ESR signals increased significantly after demethylation, confirming radical generation. TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 showed significantly enhanced ESR signal intensity. Photothermal testing used an 808 nm laser with 0.8 W cm⁻² power. Temperature was monitored via IR thermal camera. For evaporation, the foam was floated on water. The system was irradiated for 1 hour to reach equilibrium temperature.

Key Results
TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited no fluorescent emission in film, with PLQY lower than 1%. Specific PLQY values were 0.1%, 0.9%, 1.0%, and 0.3% for the four radicals. Under 808 nm laser, TPA-TPA-O6 temperature rose from 25 °C to 210 °C in 60 s. At 1.0 W cm⁻², TPA-TPA-O6 reached 250 °C within 60 s. TPA-TPA-O6 showed excellent stability over ten cycles of laser irradiation. The equilibrium temperature of PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam was 45 °C under 1 sun. This was about 10 °C higher than the PU foam alone. The water evaporation rate was 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹. The solar-driven water evaporation efficiency was 89.41%. Seawater desalination showed significant reduction in Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+, and K+ concentrations. The evaporation efficiency is among the top for pure organic small molecules.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
High spin concentration leads to highly nonradiative decay. Restricted radiative decay enhances photothermal conversion efficiency. The strong donor-acceptor conjugation reduces optical bandgap and determines paramagnetic property. The stability is attributed to rich resonance structures. This provides a novel strategy for designing stable organic photothermal materials. The materials offer a solution to the instability of traditional open-shell radicals. The design allows for structural optimization and scalable production.

Contradictions And Limitations
TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 showed lower photothermal performance due to lower spin concentration. These materials might be partially protonated, affecting performance. The study focuses on small-scale evaporation; large-scale application is not tested. Long-term stability in real-world seawater conditions is not fully detailed. The synthesis requires air oxidation, which might be sensitive to environmental conditions.

Claims
Aromatic nitric acid radicals exhibit high stability and efficient photothermal conversion. The radicals show high electrochemical and thermal stability. TPA-TPA-O6 achieves 89.41% evaporation efficiency. The materials have restricted radiative decay. Some variants like TPA-TPZ-O6 show lower performance. These materials are suitable for solar water evaporation. They offer a stable alternative to inorganic photothermal agents.
High spin concentration correlates with enhanced photothermal performance. TPA-TPA-O6 has high spin concentration and high temperature rise. Nonradiative decay is boosted by radical spin. Lower spin concentration in TPA-PY-O8 leads to lower temperature rise. Designing molecules with higher spin density can improve photothermal efficiency.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information is available free of charge at pubs.acs.org.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compares four different core structures to assess performance. TPA-TPA-O6 outperforms others due to wider absorption and higher spin. Stability was tested over ten laser cycles.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the structures of the four ANAR materials. Figure 2 presents UV-Vis absorption spectra of precursors and radicals. Figure 3 displays cyclic voltammetry curves. Figure 4 shows ESR spectra and PLQY data. Figure 5 illustrates photothermal temperature changes. Figure 6 details the evaporation system and efficiency. Table S1 lists HOMO/LUMO levels and PLQY values. Table S2 compares evaporation efficiency with other materials.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the synthesis of stable, high-spin aromatic nitric acid radicals for photothermal use. 2. The strongest evidence is the 89.41% evaporation efficiency and 210 °C temperature rise of TPA-TPA-O6. 3. The future path involves developing ANARs with enhanced planarity for electronics and spintronics.
